                    ### Question
                    A 29-year-old woman, obese, with no history of interest, who consulted for a bilateral, intense, pulsatile headache lasting one month, accompanied by horizontal diplopia and episodes of monocular amaurosis of seconds duration. The exploration is normal, except for the presence of bilateral papilledema. Which of these tests do you think will allow you to fully confirm your diagnosis ?:

                    ### Options

opb. Magnetic resonance of the skull.
opc. Electroencephalogram.
opd. Lumbar puncture.
ope. Visual evoked potentials.

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
For a patient presenting with symptoms indicative of increased intracranial pressure, such as bilateral intense pulsatile headache, horizontal diplopia, monocular amaurosis, and bilateral papilledema, the most appropriate diagnostic tests are Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) of the skull and lumbar puncture. MRI is essential for visualizing intracranial structures to identify any underlying causes of the symptoms, while lumbar puncture can confirm increased cerebrospinal fluid pressure, directly supporting a diagnosis of intracranial hypertension. Other tests like visual evoked potentials, ultrasound of supra-aortic trunks, and EEG are less relevant for confirming this specific diagnosis.
